title: Design the boundary before replacing the container
description: Choose a workload, write location, network scope, and runtime controls. Then replace the container to see which state and exposure survive the lifecycle transition.

workloads.label: Public stateless API
workloads.detail: Serves internet traffic, keeps durable state elsewhere, and peaks near 320 MB of memory.

workloads.label: Project database
workloads.detail: Must retain database files across replacement and only needs project-network callers.

workloads.label: Local development server
workloads.detail: Needs live host source edits and browser access from the Docker host.

storageOptions.label: Container writable layer
storageOptions.detail: Private to one container and removed with it.

storageOptions.label: Named volume
storageOptions.detail: Docker-managed storage with a lifecycle independent of one container.

storageOptions.label: Bind mount
storageOptions.detail: A specific daemon-host path appears inside the container.

storageOptions.label: tmpfs mount
storageOptions.detail: Temporary memory-backed files disappear after stop or restart.

networkModes.label: No network
networkModes.detail: No external network interface is attached.

networkModes.label: User-defined bridge only
networkModes.detail: Named peers on the same Docker host can connect; no host port is published.

networkModes.label: Bridge published to 127.0.0.1
networkModes.detail: The Docker host can connect through one loopback-bound published port.

networkModes.label: Bridge published on all interfaces
networkModes.detail: External clients can reach an explicitly published host port when host policy allows it.

networkModes.label: Host network
networkModes.detail: The container shares the host network namespace and its port space.
